title: Gift cards and the simple version
metaTitle: Gift cards, said simply or removed
excerpt: If you sell gift cards, say what they can buy and when they expire before someone pays. If you do not sell them, remove the gift link instead of leaving a control that fails.
alt: A two-lane road through red rock, with a single car far ahead and a mountain at the end. A simple route, which is all a gift card path should ask of someone.
caption: One road, and a clear end to it. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What must a gift card page say?
faqs.answer: Say what the card can buy, where it works, when the recipient receives it, and when it expires. Fixed amounts are easier to understand than an open field that fails after submit. If a remainder stays on the code, say that before anyone tries to spend part of it.

faqs.question: Should a digital gift card use the normal checkout?
faqs.answer: No. Do not ask for a shipping address to send an email. Ask for the recipient, a from-name, an optional note, and the buyer's email, then payment. Show the total before the card number, and do not force an account before the gift can be bought.

faqs.question: What if we do not offer gift cards?
faqs.answer: Remove the word from the footer, the account menu, and any payment field that always errors. A missing feature is fine. A feature that looks real and breaks makes the rest of the shop feel unfinished. Coupons and gift cards should not share one unlabeled box if you offer both.

markdown:
Gift card checkout UX is a small product with a few facts that must be true: what the card can buy, where it can be used, and when it expires. If you offer cards, say those facts before someone pays. If you do not offer them, remove the gift option from the footer, the bag, and the help menu. A control that leads nowhere feels like the rest of the shop might be unfinished too.

Treat the card as its own product page, not as a code field someone might notice. The buyer of a gift and the person who receives it are different readers. Write for both, in that order.

## Say what the card is, in one screen

The page needs a plain definition. “A digital card for our shop. The recipient gets a code by email and can spend it on any in-stock product.” Add the limits in the same block. Not valid on shipping. Not valid on another gift card. Valid only in this country. One brand, not a marketplace of other brands. If a limit exists, it is part of the definition, not a footnote on a PDF.

Show amounts as choices you actually support. Fixed values are easier to understand than an open box, unless you truly accept any amount in a range. If you use a range, show the minimum and the maximum next to the field. A field that fails after submit with “amount not allowed” has wasted the only moment the buyer was ready.

Say when the recipient receives it. “Email within a few minutes” or “Email on the date you choose, in the morning of that day in Eastern time.” A scheduled gift that arrives late is a failed gift, even if the code is valid. If you cannot schedule, do not show a date picker from the platform default.

Expiration belongs here, before purchase. “Expires five years from purchase” or “Does not expire.” If the law where you sell sets a minimum, follow it and say the rule in human time. “See terms” is not an expiration. People will assume the worst, or they will assume never, and either mistake becomes a support ticket.

## The buyer’s checkout should stay short

The gift card is the whole order for many buyers. Do not make them walk a shipping form to send an email. Ask for the recipient’s email, a from-name, and an optional note. Ask for the buyer’s email for the receipt. Then payment.

[Baymard Institute](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) reports an average documented cart abandonment rate of 70.22 percent across fifty studies, updated in September 2025. In the reasons study on that page, 17 percent of US online shoppers had abandoned because the checkout felt too long or complicated, and 17 percent had hit errors or a crash. A gift card flow that reuses the physical-product checkout, with an address and a shipping method for an email, is that kind of length. Baymard’s checkout benchmark also notes that an ideal flow can be as short as 12 to 14 form elements. A card that needs five facts should not inherit twenty.

Show the total before the card number. A digital delivery fee, if you charge one, is an extra cost and belongs in the open. Most shops should not charge one. If the amount on the button matches the value of the gift, say that. “$100 card, $100 charged.” Fees that appear later make the gift feel smaller than the buyer meant, which is a miserable surprise.

Let them buy without creating an account unless they need an account to manage the card later. Offer to save the order after payment. A password wall in front of a gift is how a last-minute buyer gives up and leaves your site for a marketplace that will not make them register.

Confirm on the page and in the buyer’s email. The confirmation should say the amount, the recipient address, and whether the gift has been sent or is scheduled. Do not include the redeemable code in the buyer’s email if the recipient is supposed to receive it separately. Do include a way for the buyer to see that the send succeeded.

## What the recipient must be able to do

The recipient’s email is the product. Name the shop, the amount, who it is from, and the note. Show the code in text they can copy, not only inside an image. Say where to enter it. “At checkout, in the gift card field.” Link to the shop, ideally to a collection, not to your homepage hero with no path.

Say expiration again. Say what happens to a remainder. “A balance stays on the code until it is used or it expires.” If you do not support partial redemption, say that before they try, in this email and on the redeeming checkout. A code that fails halfway through a purchase feels like a scam even when the cause is a rule you never wrote down.

If the code fails, the error should say why, in the checkout, next to the field. Wrong code, expired, already empty, or not valid on this product. A red field with “invalid” forces them to write to you. You will answer the same four cases forever. Write them once, in the product.

Do not require the recipient to create an account to see the balance. A balance check with the code, on a simple page, is enough. If you do want an account, make it optional and explain what it adds. The gift should not depend on a login the giver never mentioned.

## If you do not sell cards, delete the ghost

Platforms leave “gift card” in footers, in the account menu, and as a payment method that errors. Click every one of those before you launch. If the destination is an empty collection, a 404, or a field that always fails, remove the link. A missing feature is fine. A feature that looks real and breaks is a trust problem on the pages that do work.

Search your templates for the words gift, voucher, and coupon. They are different tools. A coupon is a promotion. A gift card is stored value. Mixing the fields in one input is how a promo code overwrites a balance or a balance is rejected as “code not found.” If you offer both, use two labeled fields, or one field that detects both and says which one it accepted.

Staff should know the answer when someone asks. Write a three-line macro that matches the page. Amounts you sell, how to send, how to redeem, who to write if the email never arrived. A macro that contradicts the product page will be copied into replies, and then you will have two policies.

Physical cards, if you ever add them, are a different product: inventory, a mail window, and a code that is not live until delivery. Do not promise a physical card with the digital flow. If you only do digital, say digital in the name and in the first sentence so nobody waits for an envelope.

## Balance, refunds, and the awkward cases

Decide the refund rule before the first angry email. If a product bought with a gift card is returned, does the value go back to the code, to the buyer, or to store credit? Say it in the policy and in the return flow. A refund to a card the recipient does not control, or to a buyer who has disappeared, will sit in your queue.

Lost email: the buyer should be able to resend from the receipt, or a person on your team should be able to resend without minting a second balance. Two codes for one payment is a real loss. Log the send. Keep one source of truth for the balance.

Fraud and mistakes: a buyer who types the wrong recipient address needs a window to correct it before the code is used. Say whether you can void and resend. If you cannot, say that the address cannot be changed after send, and make them confirm the address on the page. Confirmation checkboxes are easy to click through. Showing the address in a sentence, “We will send this to ada@…”, is harder to miss.

Expiration reminders are optional and dangerous if they are wrong. If you send one, send it only for cards with a real balance, with the real date, and with the code or a safe way to see it. A reminder for a card that was spent last year looks careless.

Tax on the purchase of the card, and tax on the later redemption, should follow the rules where you sell. Do not invent a friendly version. Your payment provider’s documentation is the parent. The page only needs the sentence the buyer must see, reviewed by whoever owns the books.

## Check the path with two inboxes

Buy the smallest card from a phone, with a recipient address you control. Read the buyer email and the recipient email. Redeem the code on a cheap product. Then try to redeem it again and read the error. Check the balance page. Click every gift link in the footer.

You are done when a giver can explain the card in one breath, and a recipient can spend it without writing to you. Anything you cannot demonstrate, take off the page.

A gift card is a one-time amount. A subscription is a repeating shipment, and it needs a different kind of honesty about the second charge. [Subscriptions for a physical product](/blog/subscriptions-for-a-physical-product) is the next piece if you are deciding whether “send this every month” belongs in the same shop.

For a storefront where the small utilities are designed with the same care as the campaign pages, look at [Hanabi’s selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The projects show how a shop is put together, including the unglamorous paths.
